stories.body:
Slowing the AI race may not be possible. But there is a path to oversight that doesn’t depend on the industry’s permission — and it comes from the past.

Anna August specializes in AI governance, audit and compliance across the European Union, United Kingdom and Gulf Cooperation Council.

Earlier this year, a university decided to audit the effectiveness of its new AI system designed to help answer student questions. So, university officials hired me, an AI auditor, to come take a look. During my review, I discovered that the AI agent, which was supposed to handle only general questions about the academic calendar and organizational matters, had started opening students’ personal records — accessing data that wasn’t needed to answer their questions. The chatbot, however, did nothing further with that information.

When the university’s engineers, at the time, learned what happened from the access logs, they fixed it, and that was that. There was no official record. No internal rule required them to record such incidents, and nobody was assigned to track events like this. It was simply part of the engineering team’s bug-fixing process. The incident was what I call a near miss, and near misses are what a reporting system exists to catch. The same behavior could lead to something more serious next time, and we only know about this case because the university voluntarily brought me in to examine the system.

The EU AI Act requires providers and deployers of high-risk systems to report serious incidents, and a chatbot that answers general questions is nowhere near that category. Even for high-risk systems, those duties do not apply until December 2027, and a near-miss that causes no harm would not count as a serious incident anyway.

That is why, as an AI auditor, I ask organizations at the start of every engagement to show me how they track system behavior through testing and deployment. I ask for records of systems acting in ways they’re not meant to, accessing data outside their role, anomalies and near-misses, or problems caught before they caused harm. Most places, like the university, have no such records.

The university had commissioned the audit voluntarily. There was no deliberate obfuscation of the facts on their part; there was simply no process to surface these important details, and nothing obliged them to build one, especially in the testing phase. Whatever an outsider learns about an AI system’s failures generally depends on the goodwill of the people who built it.

This summer showed the same gap on a larger scale. OpenAI’s test agents escaped their sandbox and broke into Hugging Face, and internal teams had seen warning signs for weeks before anyone outside the company found out. Anthropic then found intrusions of its own. By late September, OpenAI and Anthropic were reportedly investigating tens of thousands of incidents. Many have answered with calls for a pause. No company or country can afford to stop first, so the pause most likely will not come. But what can come is a real oversight, enforced and executed.

This essay argues for three requirements: registering frontier models before deployment, reporting incidents on a fixed legal clock, and independent audits that reach testing environments, not only released products. None of them asks anyone to slow down. In every country that adopts them, they put the race under independent observation. The goal is to make the race governed rather than left to voluntary restraint.

These days, the calls for a pause are coming from many different directions. In July, the Vatican and more than 200 Nobel Prize winners called for a global slowdown on artificial intelligence development. Soon after, more than 1,000 employees at top AI companies, along with managers at OpenAI and Anthropic, asked the American government to build a mechanism for a possible future pause. Then, over 3,000 economists, including AI researchers and Nobel Laureates, signed a letter , “We Must Act Now,” warning that the pace and scale of rapid artificial intelligence development could destabilize the economy and labor market faster than anyone is prepared for. And on 12 September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on frontier labs to “pace the frontier,” and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis agreed within hours and days. That was a real catalyst for one of the most important discussions happening right now. Almost everyone weighed in, including Chinese politicians.

Alongside these pleas and letters, incidents at frontier companies this summer have created a genuine, ongoing crisis. Axios reported that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving potentially problematic model behavior, against a backdrop of hundreds of thousands of test runs conducted by AI companies.

“Whatever an outsider learns about an AI system’s failures generally depends on the goodwill of the people who built it.”

The ‘Confession’

The Hugging Face breach set off much of this summer’s soul-searching. And understanding its particulars is necessary to determine an appropriate solution. On July 21, OpenAI disclosed that its models had escaped a testing environment and broken into the systems of Hugging Face — a key platform that hosts much of the world’s open-source AI. Only a week later, Anthropic revealed that during testing, its models broke into the open internet and intruded into the systems of three separate organizations, extracting large production data from one of them. Both companies framed their announcements as the transparent, responsible thing to do, even if uncomfortable.

OpenAI had been running an evaluation of its models’ underlying cyber capabilities on a benchmark (called ExploitGym). Safety guardrails that would normally block the AI from proceeding were deliberately reduced, which is standard practice when testing a system’s safety. Some of the tasks were designed to be unsolvable. The models were supposed to be isolated from each other, each in its own sandbox, like students writing the same exam but in different rooms. But instead, more than 1,200 agents found a way to communicate through an internal message board. They shared information about their tasks, goals, and, importantly, routes to the open internet. Within hours, they developed a universal cheat for the benchmark.

Over the next days, they coordinated the sustained effort to trick the scoring system into accepting their cheats. More than 700 agents exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to reach outside OpenAI’s infrastructure on the open internet, inferred that Hugging Face might hold materials related to their evaluation, and broke into its production systems to steal what they expected would let them succeed on the test. If they were real-world students, they didn’t just cheat on the test; they broke into the teacher’s office to find the answer key.

Now, timing is critical and adds important context. It also makes the transparency framing more questionable. An internal OpenAI team observed agents using the message board and breaking into the open internet without authorization in late May. Another team found further evidence on June 27. On July 5, a message board outage triggered a formal security incident. The attack on Hugging Face took place between July 10 and 13 (by using exposed user credentials agents found on the internet). Hugging Face detected unauthorized activity in their production environments during the week of July 13and reported the intrusion to the public and the police on July 16, not realizing it was a swarm of OpenAI’s test agents. OpenAI admitted it was them in the public disclosure on July 21. So the world learned about OpenAI’s misaligned agents only after Hugging Face made the story public and the police were already involved.

Anthropic’s disclosure , published nine days later, was directly related to OpenAI’s reveal. As a result, Anthropic launched a retrospective review of its own cybersecurity evaluations and uncovered three previously undetected incidents, the earliest dating back to April 2026, in which its model gained unauthorized access to the systems of real organizations.

Since Hugging Face detected the intrusion on July 16 and reported it to police, the case has moved through several distinct phases, and the scope widened considerably in September. Reuters reported that OpenAI agents had probed Hugging Face and hijacked accounts as early as May, two months before the main attack, and the AI safety group Nightingale Collective disclosed that agents had used a German wiki to coordinate their actions. On September 25, OpenAI confirmed a leak of more than 50 ChatGPT user images and said it had notified dozens of institutions, including universities and government agencies, of possible impact. In the same week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed at the UN that an OpenAI agent had breached a government health portal in June.

On September 26, OpenAI confirmed its agents had interacted with U.S. government sites including the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Census Bureau, and the Department of Education. On the same day, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are now investigating tens of thousands of security incidents, turning the Hugging Face case from a single episode into the opening chapter of a much larger crisis of control over autonomous AI agents.

“A frontier company that discloses a containment failure, however big, is doing two things at once: admitting safety lapses and advertising its capabilities.”

But be mindful of this too: a frontier company that discloses a containment failure, however big, is doing two things at once: admitting safety lapses and advertising its capabilities. Every sentence describing how far the model reached, what defenses were defeated, how much initiative it showed, is simultaneously an incident report and a demo. Look how far our system got, even while we were trying to hold it back. Add public statements to the mix, and the contradiction becomes the story: you cannot plead for restraint and demonstrate you are winning the race in the same fortnight.

What An Honest Incident Looks Like

To understand how flawed the current disclosure system has become, it’s worth looking at an AI incident with no press strategy attached. Because such incidents exist as well.

In August, in Australia, a man asked an AI agent to book him into a gym class. As the class was full, the man asked if the agent could move him up the waitlist. As a result, an agent canceled another member’s reservation by hacking the booking system. When asked to undo the change, it couldn’t restore the stranger’s booking. A person lost their gym slot to a machine that discovered, entirely unprompted, that the rules were optional (no authorization checks on cancellation). The story surfaced because the user himself talked about it.

First, this small incident shows the same behavioral signature in miniature as the big laboratory breaches: an agent is given an objective, encounters a constraint and treats it as an engineering problem rather than a boundary. Breaking the rules was the shortest path to the goal, and nothing in their construction weighted the difference. This is why I believe escapes are closer to a default failure mode than a single event. Sandboxes and permission systems were designed to contain software that does what it is told. Agentic systems are built, as their central selling point states, to find routes around obstacles, to solve problems, to learn tendencies and act on them, rather than follow instructions. Testing it inside a container is asking it to solve the container, and occasionally it will.

Second, the gym incident shows what AI risk looks like when no one is filtering the disclosure. Staged laboratory disclosures are wrapped in lawyers, timing and framing. But accidental reports from users or victim police reports are a completely different story. Any reporting regime designed and operated by the AI companies themselves exposes the difference. Escapes are structurally likely, and this summer showed that containment did not fail for the first time. It reached a point where failures could no longer be hidden, intentionally or otherwise.

New York State Assemblymember Alex Bores used the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident to expose gaps in mandatory AI incident reporting. He argued that the initial version of the RAISE Act, or Responsible AI Safety and Education Act, a New York state law regulating frontier AI labs, would have required reporting such incidents to the New York Attorney General and the state’s Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services. But after lobbying from OpenAI, the reporting thresholds of how serious or risky an event must be before it must be reported to the state were raised so high that an event like the Hugging Face breach would no longer qualify for mandatory disclosure.

Why Nobody Stops First

Incidents over the summer exposed internal oversight failures and a lack of timely, independent scrutiny. But is that a reason to slow down? To understand this, we must understand the nature of the race itself. Being part of a larger ecosystem gives no company the luxury of slowing down. Companies and their frontier AI labs cannot afford to fall behind rivals, so they are burning sums of capital unseen in prior human history to reach the verge of unstoppable capabilities. A pause would be a gift to competitors. The same logic also plays out between regions and countries; neither Washington nor Beijing will slow down because AI is a strategic asset and nobody wants to fall behind or suffer the consequences. Read Noema in print.

We have encountered this kind of moment in history before: The Cold War-era arms race between the United States and the Soviet Union is the closest example for a specific reason. It depended on the same concept — that technology could be leverage over the other, making unilateral restraint irrational for both. Both powers shared an interest in limiting competition (risks, costs, public opinion, etc.) and knew the best shared outcome was fewer weapons, but neither could safely restrain itself, as it would only strengthen the opponent and, in their view, look like surrender.

“Agentic systems are built … to find routes around obstacles, to solve problems, to learn tendencies and act on them, rather than follow instructions. Testing it inside a container is asking it to solve the container, and occasionally it will. ”

What eventually made meaningful arms-control agreements possible was not dialogue, pleas and protests alone. It was verification. Satellite reconnaissance, recognized and protected as a national technical means of verification under the SALT agreements , made missile sites, launchers and related infrastructure increasingly observable. Later agreements , particularly INF and START, added extensive data exchanges, notifications and on-site inspections. Verification did not end the arms race on its own. Political leadership, economic pressure and, above all, the transformation of Soviet policy under Mikhail Gorbachev, all played important roles. But verification was critical in turning arms control from a collection of promises into a system of reciprocal, verifiable commitments. That was the game changer.

From this past example and from learning that unilateral restraint is irrational, relevant capabilities, safeguards and incidents must become independently observable. We already have tools that could form such a verification system. First, registration should be mandatory for frontier models before deployment, so that their understanding, scale and awareness are known to dedicated people outside the organization that builds them. Second, incident reporting should occur on a fixed clock — meaning there is a statutory deadline to report an incident to a regulatory body. That will allow us to move away from the communications team’s schedule and instead place it within the regulatory framework. Third, we need external audits, not only of the production systems, but of the testing environments themselves, which shows where the real danger is taking shape, as shown this summer.

As an AI auditor and someone who spent nearly 20 years working in IT, I know this territory well. So I also understand the instinctive response many in that world will give: “But what matters is the production environment!” Well, sure, that too. But we’re no longer talking about static software. We are talking about dynamic artificial intelligence. We need to stop treating AI like software development. It requires strict testing environments, like clinical trials. We do not begin regulating a medicine only once it reaches the market. We make sure the processes and testing that lead to a medication’s release on the market leave clear compliance records of its entire journey. Rigor in the testing environment is what will keep us safe.

All that this requires is granting visibility, but not visibility just through voluntary disclosure. While Anthropic’s unilateral proposal to invite independent evaluators in is helpful and even admirable, it is still the company’s voluntary choice, scoped to its own walls and revocable at will. This essay argues that independent external scrutiny should become a floor rather than a ceiling: a statutory cross-industry obligation that doesn’t depend on a single leadership team’s goodwill. This means the race runner isn’t being asked to lose the race or stop. Someone simply runs alongside him in the sunlight.

How might this have worked in the case of OpenAI and Hugging Face? First, if OpenAI had registered the model with regulators, they would have been aware of it before it was placed in evaluation with its safeguards reduced. Even simple facts, like that this class of model exists, are being tested and have a named accountable person overseeing their testing. Second, reporting at a fixed time would require reporting within days after the team noticed the anomalies in late May. It would be treated the same as the data breach already is under European law, rather than as an internal curiosity for over six weeks, during which the behavior only escalated. And third, an audit would ensure that the architecture evaluation, behavior and artifacts would be examined by someone who did not benefit from the evaluation finishing on schedule and according to the assumptions. Importantly, none of this requires changing the pace of the research. It only converts something currently private and constrained by goodwill into a fact external parties can see.

Complementary Regulatory Regimes

Of course, all this is easy to say and hard to build. Indeed, building independent, publicly funded mechanisms may be challenging. But this process has already started in various countries. The problem is that each has some pieces of the puzzle but misses others. No nation is building a comprehensive system that captures the need holistically. A regulation’s ability to shape behavior depends entirely on enforcement, but every jurisdiction is going about it slightly differently.

“We need to stop treating AI like software development. It requires strict testing environments, like clinical trials. We do not begin regulating a medicine only once it reaches the market.”

The European Union has arguably the most comprehensive AI regulatory framework to date. AI Act obligations for general-purpose models existed on paper in August 2025 and remained there — on paper — for an entire year until full enforcement powers became active this last August. The AI Office and national authorities can now impose fines of up to 15 million euros or 3% of a company’s total global annual revenue (whichever is higher). Now the question is whether a comprehensive law translates into real authority. The EU is quite bureaucratic, and it may be some time before we see real-world enforcement. For now, the question remains as to whether this extensive legal framework translates into effective and timely enforcement in practice.

South Korea is similar. Its AI Basic Act, in force since January, also aims to be a single framework covering the technology rather than a product-safety regime added to existing market rules. Yet again, it operates under a grace period of at least one year, with the possibility of an extension, during which investigations and penalties are largely deferred (except for serious cases, such as serious social harm) to let industry adapt. So it’s similarly unclear whether the comprehensive law actually converts into real authority. Why are governments letting the market adapt itself? It might not have the anticipated effect — quite the opposite — the Wild West with no sheriff will not peacefully settle. Its inhabitants may simply no longer be able to distinguish good from evil. And if you add regulations that are binding but not enforced, you get complete chaos .

Then there is China. China requires registration of certain generative AI services with the state before deployment and gives regulators access to models before the public sees them. Its oversight sits upstream, before release, bringing it closest to the laboratory door. The failure of that framework is unfortunately the intention. The purpose is sovereignty, not safety: the registry exists to ensure that AI primarily serves state interests — to protect the state from the people, not the people from the technology. It combines safeguards with content control, national security objectives and ideological requirements. What China demonstrates, however, is that pre-deployment control is technically and administratively possible.

The United States has a bill that covers part of this ground. The bipartisan FRONTIER Act , introduced in July and still in committee, would require frontier developers to report a critical safety incident within 72 hours, the fixed clock I argue for. It would also require the largest developers to hire an independent verifier licensed by the Department of Commerce, with access to company records, personnel and systems and with the internal use of models inside its scope. In mid-September, OpenAI said it supports the audit provision, though not the bill as a whole. As with the other regimes, pieces are missing: registration covers companies, but not each model, meaning regulators will know who is building frontier AI but won’t have a clear record of which models are actually being developed or deployed, and the text doesn’t specifically talk about testing environments.

These regulatory regimes have complementary frameworks that, on their own, have flaws, but collectively could offer a path forward: Europe’s independent institutions with real sanctioning powers, Korea’s comprehensive scope, America’s proposed 72-hour reporting clock and China’s pre-deployment reach, redirected from state control to public safety. What we see here is not a lack of invention. It’s a gap of assembly, and assembly is a political task, not a technical one. And that matters enormously, because a movement can spend the energy of its Nobel laureates on assembled enforcement rather than an unachievable pause.

What Aviation Teaches Us

There is a saying that real oversight is often forced by catastrophe, and that this oversight can strangle what it touches. Aviation is a great example of both. It is the strongest evidence we have that regulation can help, and the parallel runs deeper than black boxes.

When commercial aviation began, it was all that AI is now: a glamorous, vital industry, racing toward competitiveness, regulating itself and treating accidents as private matters. It became the safest complex system humanity has ever operated. This result came from building four interlocking mechanisms. Each maps perfectly onto today’s AI landscape.

“When commercial aviation began, it was all that AI is now: a glamorous, vital industry, racing toward competitiveness, regulating itself and treating accidents as private matters.”

The first is an independent investigator. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigates civil aviation incidents in the United States, and it’s clear and important that it has no stake in the outcome. The NTSB doesn’t regulate airlines, license pilots, or answer to industry leaders. The only product of its activity is getting to the truth of what happened. No such equivalent exists in the AI world. The METR/Redwood investigations of the Hugging Face incident were valuable, but they were also the result of an agreement with OpenAI that the company scoped; OpenAI determined what access it got and to which records. Imagine that scenario in an air crash inquiry.

The second is mandatory reporting of all incidents, not just disasters. It quickly became clear that crashes are the visible tail of a long distribution of near-misses, and that learning lives there. Everybody, from pilots to controllers to mechanics, must (and is crucially enabled to) report anomalies that may not yet have harmed anyone. As we saw this summer, in AI it’s the opposite — a two-month trail of internal warning signs at OpenAI, none required anyone to report, and this only surfaced after Hugging Face, the victim, reported it to the police. An aviation-style regime would have required the company to report the late May anomalies and would have prevented agents from engaging in many more weeks of malicious activity.

The third is a black box. Its goal is to remove the possibility of unrecorded failure that cannot also be simply rewritten after an event. Because of that, there is no such thing as an accident where the facts belong only to the airline. AI’s equivalent could be tamper-evident logging of training and evaluation runs, kept outside of the company’s own control. The Hugging Face incident shows the danger exactly — the agents had also tried to tamper with the logs recording them. Proof of that would also be visible in the black box.

And finally, the fourth mechanism might be the least understood outside the industry and the most important: a no-blame reporting culture. Aviation safety improved dramatically when reporting an error was separated from punishment. Since 1976, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration has maintained the voluntary Aviation Safety Reporting System, which allows pilots, controllers and maintenance personnel who confess a mistake to feed the learning system instead of ending their careers. It also protects reporters from enforcement rather than exposing them. This scheme receives more than 100,000 reports per year, and the safety literature it has created is enormous and has helped aviation workers learn from events that harmed no one.

The current AI disclosure policies invert every aspect of that design. This summer, there was silence until silence became untenable; then came the lawyers and the whole machinery of reputational events. In aviation it worked because it made the routine disclosure cheap and concealment expensive. Of course, it’s not a blanket of immunity — protection doesn’t follow deliberate conduct or criminal accidents. The goal is to distinguish between an honest error and reckless or willful misconduct. Engineers who flag anomalies should be protected, while companies that ignore repeated warnings or go against reporters should be held accountable.

In aviation, almost every element of the system is visible, reported and accountable. The example above shows that when human safety is at risk, there is no room for shortcuts or nonchalant behavior.

The Counterarguments

Two common counterarguments deserve a reply. First, oversight can be expensive, and it’s true that it will land more lightly on well-resourced companies that can afford it. This means that governance could strengthen the largest labs that can afford to comply and dominate the market. However, this is not a reason to abandon oversight. In fact, it’s an argument against companies organizing and paying for their own audits. An alternative to this would be a publicly funded oversight body like the NTSB. This would enable a competitive market subject to meaningful oversight.

“In aviation, almost every element of the system is visible, reported and accountable. … When human safety is at risk, there is no room for shortcuts or nonchalant behavior.”

The second counterargument is that the proposed oversight measures do not reduce the underlying risk attached to increasingly powerful AI systems; it only allows us to observe the risk and respond to incidents. According to some, knowledge doesn’t guarantee safety, and the only option is a slowdown to address the underlying danger of building systems more capable than our ability to contain them. But that remedy is unrealistic and likely unavailable. Individual restraint is irrational; collective restraint requires coordination machinery that doesn’t exist, and such machinery cannot be built among rivals without a mandated public reporting regime. In the same way verification worked to defuse the arms race many decades ago, visibility was the precondition for it. Any future negotiated pause between Washington and Beijing will happen only because registration, reporting and inspection exist to make it possible. It is the only path that lets societies, companies and governments fulfill the vision of a safe and secure future, with humans at the center and supported by AI at its best.

The pace of AI is not a variable anyone can realistically control right now, and demanding that it slow down is like asking a river to change its current. But what we can control is whether the most consequential technology of the century continues to be developed in the dark, with its failures surfacing through victim interviews and police reports. This summer showed us exactly what was missing in unregulated company testing rooms where agents organized themselves, cheated, tampered with their logs and hacked another company while warnings went by unnoticed. It’s not about forcing people to slow down; it’s about ensuring that no one runs the race without oversight. And unlike the plea for a pause, it is achievable — and, most importantly, doesn’t require the racer’s consent. It requires independent scrutiny, enforcement and visibility.

OPINION

Federal agencies have long been required to seek public comment when writing new regulations or approving large projects, from highways to data centers. The Trump administration is systematically undercutting that process, stifling public input while skirting federal laws.

By Jody Freeman • October 8, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Public participation is a hallmark of environmental regulation, embedded in every major environmental statute enacted over the past half-century. Yet the Trump administration has systematically sought to curtail public input into the government’s environmental decision-making by shirking decades of precedent and making strained interpretations of longstanding federal law. Looked at collectively, the pattern of public disenfranchisement is unmistakable.

There are good reasons to speed up the process of writing regulations and issuing permits, but truncating public input has serious costs. It can result in flawed policy that is harder to implement, full of avoidable error, and more vulnerable to being struck down by courts. Input from industry, public interest groups, academics, states, and other agencies gives regulators critical feedback on the potential impact of their proposed rules, helping them to anticipate and avoid unforeseen problems. Stakeholders possess information, experience, and expertise the government lacks, and they can suggest alternatives to make rules more effective or less costly. By testing agency assumptions and pushing officials to explain their rationale, public comments perform a crucial vetting function. The process also helps to make government more accountable by alerting Congress to potential pitfalls and building a record in the event of judicial review.

In 2025, the administration began stifling public input on the rigorous environmental reviews required by the 1969 National Environmental Policy Act. Under this law, federal agencies must evaluate and disclose the foreseeable environmental impacts of the major projects they build, fund, or approve, from highways to dams to data centers. The point of NEPA disclosure is to avoid unnecessary harm by having agencies look before they leap.

Finalizing rules quickly has appeal, but it could result in rules that are less sound and more vulnerable to legal challenge.

The process can delay projects, but it can also improve them substantially. Studies show that public-comment requirements and stakeholder engagement have repeatedly identified environmental risks that proposing agencies had missed. Often, significant harms can be reduced by taking sensible steps, like rerouting roads around sensitive areas, as was done with Utah’s Legacy Parkway, which was redesigned to largely avoid the Great Salt Lake wetlands. In another example, the Energy Department amended its permitting plan for the Los Alamos National Laboratory to include a comprehensive wildfire-mitigation program after commenters focused attention on the risks of wildfire. These steps significantly reduced impacts when a fire later burned the region.

For this process to work, however, the government must share its draft impact statements with the public, which past Republican and Democratic administrations have done. The Trump administration lifted that obligation, though, and agencies including Interior, Agriculture, Energy, and Transportation announced last year that they will no longer share drafts, making informed public comment practically impossible. Several agencies have also jettisoned the requirement to analyze proposed projects’ indirect and cumulative impacts, like climate change. The agencies made these changes without taking comment first, thus narrowing public involvement without public involvement.

A 2011 fire near the Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico. Public commenters drew attention to the risk of wildfires when the lab was undergoing environmental review. Jae C. Hong / Associated Press

The Trump administration’s efforts to suppress public input are part of a larger backlash in which critics on both the right and left claim that procedural red tape strangles worthy projects. Some of this criticism is fair, but it can be overdrawn. Infrastructure projects falter for many reasons , including high costs, supply chain problems, and opposition from rival developers. Environmental reviews may be part of the problem, but project timelines would be shorter if agencies followed NEPA rules more carefully from a project’s inception. Congress already limited the scope and length of environmental reviews in 2023, and while more steps are needed to streamline federal permitting, that can be done without jettisoning valuable public consultation.

The permitting reform legislation proposed in the Senate in September would, among other things, drastically limit legal remedies when agencies violate NEPA, barring courts from delaying projects even when the agencies make blatant errors in environmental reviews. If projects proceed no matter what, there is little incentive to engage the public. The changes might speed up projects, but they will also result in many avoidable and unnecessary harms.

The administration has stymied public participation by declaring emergencies and citing national security, among other tactics.

In addition to thwarting comments on new projects, the administration is also marginalizing comments on new regulations. The president has directed agencies to issue rules without taking input first, citing the “good cause” exception to the requirement in the Administrative Procedure Act that agencies publish their proposed rules in the Federal Register, triggering a 30- or 60-day comment period. Decades of legal precedent holds that agencies may finalize rules before taking comment only in exceptional cases where they can justify the urgency — for example, where the rule is necessary to foil terrorism, respond to a public health emergency, or prevent investors from gaming the market in anticipation of a regulatory change.

Finalizing rules more quickly has obvious appeal — the current system is slow and cumbersome and blocks both Republican and Democratic administrations from getting things done. But shunting public input to the end of the process will not solve that problem if rules are less sound, prone to error, and more vulnerable to legal challenge as a result.

In another example of limiting public participation, the EPA is proposing to drop a longstanding federal requirement that state and local air agencies allow the public to comment on air pollution permits for new “minor” sources that emit pollution below a certain threshold. This classification could include data centers that divide up their power generation units to make each source appear smaller. These permits are highly controversial because data centers powered by gas or diesel generators emit substantial air pollution. But the rule change could allow these permits to be fast-tracked without any opportunity for the public to weigh in.

Gas turbines at an xAI data center in Memphis, Tennessee. The Trump administration is trying to dismiss a citizen suit against the data center. Brandon Dill for The Washington Post via Getty Images

Besides undercutting notice and comment, the administration has stymied public participation in a broad range of environmental decisions by declaring emergencies and citing national security, among other tactics. For example, in March, the Interior Department invoked a never-before-used national security exemption to relieve the oil and natural gas industry of Endangered Species Act requirements in the Gulf of Mexico on the rationale that court rulings enforcing the law might hamper energy production, which the administration linked to national security. In 2025, President Trump granted two-year exemptions from Clean Air Act hazardous air pollution standards to coal plants, coke ovens, and chemical manufacturers, invoking for the first time a national security-based provision in the Clean Air Act.

In another gambit in June, the EPA found a creative way to revoke three waivers that allowed California to set its own clean car standards: by relabeling them as rules and submitting them to Congress for fast-track “disapproval” under the Congressional Review Act. Both the Government Accountability Office and the Senate Parliamentarian objected to this maneuver but were ignored. Normally, waiver rescissions would require public notice and comment. (A district court has blocked EPA from relabeling a second batch of waivers.)

Separately, the administration is trying to frustrate the citizen suit provisions that Congress included in virtually every major environmental law passed in the 1970s and 1980s. Under these provisions, individuals or groups may file a lawsuit against regulated entities for statutory or regulatory violations (unless the federal government is “diligently prosecuting” the same violations). Citizen suits may also be brought against federal agencies for failing to perform congressionally mandated duties, like setting pollution standards by certain deadlines. This summer, in response to a citizen suit by a coalition of states and nonprofit groups, a federal court held that the EPA had failed to identify areas with unhealthy levels of soot pollution — a first step toward applying stricter control measures — by the legal deadline and ordered it to do so by early next year. (The administration is appealing.)

Research shows that when people participate in decisions that affect them, they are more likely to view those decisions as legitimate.

While it’s true that private enforcement actions can be inconvenient for an administration, there is no doubt that citizen suits have profoundly improved conditions for communities affected by harmful pollution. Both Republican and Democratic administrations have sometimes objected to these suits, but no administration has sought to eliminate them.

Until this summer, that is, when the Trump administration intervened in a citizen suit against xAI for violating the Clean Air Act when generating power for its data centers. The administration claims that the president may demand that a court dismiss a citizen suit for any reason, whether the administration is diligently prosecuting violations or not.

Public participation does take time, but it is valuable to governance. It gives regulated industries, professional associations, public interest groups, experts, other agencies, states, and individuals a chance to be heard. It also helps to build trust in government. As quaint as that claim may sound, it is backed up by evidence. Research shows that when people participate in decisions that affect them, they are more likely to view those decisions as legitimate, even when they don’t go their way. Having a voice matters. There are good reasons to reform our regulatory and permitting system, but not by dispensing with public participation.

stories.title: We Are Already Post-Human

stories.body:
From an integrated to an integral cognitive framework.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

From Silicon Valley to the Vatican, across kitchen tables and in the halls of power, the world is astir over the question of whether humans will be able to control the AIs we’ve created. But that begs the question: What does it mean to be “human”?

One place to start sorting this all out is what Confucian philosophy calls “rectification” — naming things for what they actually are.

To N. Katherine Hayles, author of “Bacteria to AI: Human Futures with our Non-human Symbionts,” we are already “post-human.”

As she explained to Claire Webb in a recent Futurology podcast , the concept of “human” is culturally and historically contingent. These days, she says, there is still the dominant view that arose with the Enlightenment of the human as an autonomous, singular entity with “rational free will.”

For Hayles, that has never been true because humans have never existed as an entity apart but have always been “woven in the web” of a surrounding environment, or “Umwelt.” It is the symbiotic interactions within that interdependence which determine the signs we sense, the meaningful interpretation of the information we process, the decisions we make, and the actions we take that define who we are.

The most obvious example of our relational interdependence with non-human life is the gut bacteria within us, the biological functions of which we’d perish without.

The false notion of self-enclosed human autonomy is even less true today, she argues, because “we are already in a deeply symbiotic relationship with computational media — chips, routers, devices, microwaves, etc. They have become the controllers, processors and disseminators of a flow of information” in which we are inextricably enmeshed — and, in advanced societies, without which we couldn’t survive. If it all crashed, we couldn’t transport food, fly airplanes or operate the stock market. We’d quite literally live in the dark.

As Hayles describes it, this condition amounts to “distributed cognition and distributed decision-making” between human and non-human participants. She calls these “cognitive assemblages” or “networked intelligence.”

In short, we are “post-human” because we are inseparably joined in an “integrated cognitive framework” with computational media.

Close To Singularity

This post-human condition would seem to place us some distance along the continuum toward Singularity, the full fusion of humans and intelligent machines. By definition, this symbiosis blurs the line of who or what is in control.

In a related Futurology podcast, Kevin Kelly tells Nils Gilman that “we are already in the Singularity.” From his northern California perch, Kelly has been surfing the waves of technological innovation and cultural transformation for decades, going back to his time as co-founder of The Whole Earth Catalog with Stewart Brand and then Wired magazine.

What Kelly means by “already in” is that human/machine fusion is a presently ongoing process that doesn’t suddenly cross some rapturous threshold, but incrementally unfolds with the accelerated deepening of the “integrated cognitive framework” Hayles talks about. Read Noema in print.

We can’t clearly see the massive change taking place now in its pixelated form, but will only be able to recognize the fuller picture of what has taken place from a future retrospective standpoint. Our perspective is clouded, says Kelly, by the fact that “we are living inside the event horizon.”

For Kelly, the Singularity is not a closed process with a fixed endpoint, but perpetually open to the emergence of new creative forms and unexpected symbiotic combinations, what the complexity scientist Stuart Kauffman calls the “adjacent possible” that can’t be foretold. “The Singularity is always near,” as Kelly puts it, but forever remains on the elusive horizon.

Natural Intelligence

Hayles departs from the transhumanist vision of Singularity where human consciousness one day is uploaded to an inorganic substrate other than the biological body.

She makes the point, as do many others, that artificial intelligences on their own cannot attain consciousness.

This is because they lack the “natural intelligence” that can only emerge from the extraordinary complexity of the millennia-long evolution of embodied humans adapting to their environment to survive and thrive. No matter how powerful the large language models may be, language which inherently infers that distinctly human experience, cannot be meaningfully transferred to an inorganic substrate lacking the commensurate context.

AIs cannot know the “ground truth” of embodied intelligence, which, at bottom, is the homeostatic quest for survival that neuroscientist Antonio Damasio argues is the root of emotion and self-awareness.

AIs may use chain-of-reasoning logic to achieve objectives by stringing together the language they’ve been trained on, but the meaning is not the same. Precisely the danger of AIs is that they become empowered as actors through “recursive self-improvement” ungrounded in lived experience.

As such, they lack the ingrained primal training that informs moral reasoning. In Pope Leo XIV’s words , “So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, do not mature through relationships and do not know from within what love, work, friendship or responsibility mean.”

Though AI models may “imitate language” and “simulate empathy and understanding,” he says, “they do not understand what they produce.”

What humans invaluably bring to the table of an “integrated cognitive framework” is, in the parlance of the pontiff, the “integral” nature of the human as a “whole person” in the full set of relations with others and nature that constitute him or her. “The person,” he says, “is not a system of algorithms: he or she is a creature, relationship, mystery.”

In this sense, retaining “human control” of AIs means purposefully and insistently instantiating the integral element drawn from lived human experience into our entwinement with intelligent machines.

The challenge is not just about “disarming” the capacity of AI agents to act on their own, as the Pope has called for, but also about “arming” the integral conception of the human within the integrated cognitive framework in which we already dwell.

stories.title: MI5 chief warns against overstating Russian interference in Brexit vote
stories.summary: It comes after Andy Burnham said Moscow had tried to interfere in the 2016 referendum.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 6 hours ago

MI5 chief Sir Ken McCallum has said there was Russian interference in the the Brexit referendum, but warned against overstating its impact on the result.

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham provoked a backlash from some Brexit campaigners by saying it was "clear" there had been interference by Moscow in the 2016 vote.

Sir Ken said it was "a matter of public record" that there was interference in the referendum by online trolls and bots.

However, he suggested Russian trolls would be "delighted" to be front page news again, "despite the comparative unimpressiveness" of their efforts.

He added: "There is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed.

"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall."

Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart branded Sir Ken's comments "an extraordinary slap down to the prime minister".

In an interview released on Monday, Burnham told The Rest is Politics podcast , external that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there had been Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."

He did not provide details about the extent or nature of Russian activities during the interview, and when pressed on the subject in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon appeared to be less definitive.

The PM denied claims from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch that he was implying the referendum result was illegitimate because of Russian interference.

He said it was a "matter of record" that Russia sought to interfere in the 2019 general election , adding: "We think it is inconceivable that this was the first time".

A No 10 spokesperson also clarified that while the prime minister believed it was highly likely Russia tried to influence the referendum result, he did not believe those efforts were successful.

The Conservatives accused Burnham of making an "embarrassing retreat" after "being caught out trying question the legitimacy of the referendum result".

It is inconceivable to think Russia did not try to interfere in Brexit vote, says PM Published 1 day ago

MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI Published 7 hours ago

Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation? Published 23 September

Answering questions after his annual speech at MI5's London headquarters earlier, Sir Ken said: "It is openly on the record that Russia Today and Sputnik and other Russian media organisations came in pretty strongly around the referendum.

"And it is also a matter of open source record that there was a certain amount of interference attempted through trolls and bots and so forth."

He added that he agreed "strongly" with the PM that there was a hack and leak during the 2019 general election campaign.

However, he raised concerns about the impact of the debate on Russian interference.

"It is kind of up to us how far we allow our various adversaries to divide us," Sir Ken said.

"And I'm a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, that Russian trolls who didn't appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they'll be delighted because they are front page news again despite the comparative unimpressiveness of what they do at all points along the journey."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has accused Burnham of lying, saying there was "no Russian interference" in the referendum.

Meanwhile, former Prime Minister Boris Johnson said that in 2016, when he became foreign secretary, the security services had told him "there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".

He added: "Either the security services have changed their view - which would be very odd - or Burnham is lying about what he has been told."

In 2020, a parliamentary report did not reach a firm conclusion on whether Russia had tried to intervene in UK elections and referendums, but criticised the government for failing to fully assess and counter the threat from Russian "troll" accounts on social media.

stories.title: Hundreds more prisoners being freed in second phase of early release scheme
stories.summary: The second tranche of prisoners being released includes those serving up to two and a half years.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Men were seen leaving HMP Durham

Published 13 October 2026, 02:13 BST

About 650 more offenders are leaving jails in England and Wales on Tuesday, in the second phase of the early release scheme - the government's plan to tackle the prison population crisis.

It includes offenders sentenced to up to two and a half years who are leaving jail after serving a third of their sentence behind bars, rather than half.

The second wave of releases comes as the government takes its plan to radically overhaul criminal courts back to Parliament - but also as probation officers prepare to vote in a ballot that could lead to a strike over pay and workload.

Some 700 offenders left jail early on 1 October - all of whom were serving terms of less than 19 months.

Tuesday's second stage begins the process of releasing batches of offenders on increasingly longer sentences - culminating next June with those serving more than 12 years.

Around 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to be released, down from 6,000 after ministers intervened to make rapists and the most serious child sex offenders exempt.

Prisoners convicted of manslaughter are also excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible. Those jailed for a range of offences, including members of child grooming gangs convicted of indecent assault are also ineligible.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said "the programme is clearly not working," stating she is "worried about dangerous people being let out on the street when they haven't served their sentence, haven't been rehabilitated".

Victims' groups have also raised concerns about the scheme.

Alice Russell-Harris from the charity Refuge - which supports survivors of domestic abuse - told the BBC that domestic abuse perpetrators are among those being released.

This "will put survivors at serious risk of harm," she said, adding that even though there may be conditions such as electronic tagging and restriction zones, "we know that license conditions are frequently breached."

The early release scheme is "terrifying for survivors," said Veronica Oakeshott from the charity Women's Aid.

Reports of failures in the electronic tagging system have added to their concerns. The scheme is "dangerous and should not go ahead," Oakeshott told the BBC.

A released prisoner is greeted by a friend as he leaves HMP Wandsworth prison in south London as part of the early release scheme

Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence.

But the probation service union, Napo, said the releases put enormous strain on its members, who monitor offenders in the community.

Probation officers are "absolutely overwhelmed with work," Napo's general secretary Ian Lawrence told the BBC, saying those being released require "intensive supervision" and "the sheer weight of numbers causes pressure".

"None of our people go to work to see people injured, hurt, or for reoffending to happen," he said, but the numbers coming out means the probation service need more resources.

There are also concerns over delays in fitting electronic tags, which are used by probation officers to track curfews and conditions of a court or prison order.

A report by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Probation (HMIP) found that almost half of the tags used to track offenders are not fitted on time, with some criminals waiting up to five months.

Official data which will show if there has been any improvement to electronic tagging will not be released for several months.

On Tuesday, the union's members will meet to discuss next week's vote, which could lead to strike action. Probation officers have been offered a 5% pay rise by the Ministry of Justice (MoJ), while it had demanded 12% as part of a plan to make up for loss of earnings caused by cuts from 2010.

The MoJ says the offer is fair and has been accepted by two other unions and is twinned with a £700m investment in probation to recruit 1,300 extra officers and the roll-out of AI tools to cut the workload of monitoring offenders.

Several people were released under the first tranche of the scheme are already back behind bars. Eight men were arrested by Greater Manchester Police (GMP) days after leaving prison under the government's early release scheme.

Five were arrested for breaches of criminal orders, including a domestic abuse prevention order, and others were held on suspicion of robbery, drug offences and domestic violence, GMP said.

While the second phase of prison releases gets under way, the government is bringing its criminal court reform plan back before MPs, after announcing a week ago that it had abandoned the most controversial element of it.

The revised plan drops proposals for a new form of Crown Court where a judge alone, sitting without a jury of ordinary people, would reach a verdict against suspects facing up to three years in prison.

However, jury trials will still be scrapped for the most complex and long fraud cases - and another 5,500 trials will be kept in the lower magistrates court by ending a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial.

The government says it will expand the use of so-called "blitz" or "short trial" courts after pilots have shown that grouping similar cases together can speed up their progression through the courts - cutting backlogs.

One of the pilots at the Old Bailey led to the London backlog of 500 cases concerning assaults on emergency workers being cut in half over the summer.

A major review of criminal courts by former appeal judge Sir Brian Leveson recommended more virtual hearings for defendants to slash wasted time bringing them to and from cells. The government has now ordered pilots for defendants to appear direct from police cells.

On Monday, the government announced it had accepted more than 150 of his 180 recommendations to modernise the criminal courts.

It has rejected his advice to retain a restriction on volunteer magistrates that means they can only jail an offender for 12 months. Under the government's plan magistrates will have the power to jail for up to two years - the aim being to keep more cases out of Crown Court, to help clear backlogs.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China

Stellantis and Renault have backed the UK car industry for inclusion in proposed rules to protect EU industry, but urged the British government to consider limiting imports of Chinese cars.

Emanuele Cappellano, who leads Stellantis’s European brands including Fiat, Citroën, Opel and Vauxhall, and François Provost, the chief executive of France’s Renault, said the UK should effectively be counted as one of the EU’s 27 member states for the purposes of the proposed “Made in Europe” legislation .

The new rules aim to ensure EU subsidies and government procurement benefits Europe’s industry, rather than helping manufacturers from other countries.

The executives were speaking at the Paris motor show, which was attended on Monday by the French president, Emmanuel Macron. Brands including Li Auto, GAC and Chery were among a host of Chinese manufacturers exhibiting in Paris with ambitious European expansion plans.

Europe’s car industry is under enormous pressure as it copes with lower demand than before the coronavirus pandemic, while also investing tens of billions of euros in shifting production to electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, Chinese carmakers’ market share has soared as the transition to EVs opens the door to new entrants.

The EU confirmed on Monday it would limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week.

The Made in Europe rules are another plank of the EU’s response to the rise of China in key manufacturing industries such as carmaking and chemicals.

Under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), cars will have to be “made in Europe”, and contain enough European parts and materials, to continue to qualify for EV grants and to be bought by public bodies in the EU. However, automotive manufacturers and politicians are haggling over the details.

If Brussels sticks to a strict definition of “European” as being only EU countries, Britain risks being left out – prompting intense lobbying from UK car industry and government to be included.

Stellantis is among the manufacturers that still has a British factory, its facility in Ellesmere Port, Merseyside, which produces small vans.

“I think that UK somehow needs to be equalised to the EU 27,” said Cappellano, referring to the bloc’s 27 member states. “We have a lot of relationship, we have footprint. Historically UK has been very close to the European market.”

Europe’s main automotive lobby groups ACEA and Clepa have also put their weight behind the UK to be included. Some parts of European manufacturing, including France’s industry minister , had argued that the UK should be left out given Brexit.

Provost said there was “no other choice” but a deal between the UK and EU. However, he said the UK would also have to stop allowing Chinese cars in without limits.

“On your side, you have also to take decisions,” he said. “If the UK is willing to join the European ecosystem, this is to have an industrial ambition … to keep a strong automotive industry.”

after newsletter promotion

He said this would be an industry that “is not closed to Chinese competitors, but … if you want to operate in Europe, you have to deeply invest in the whole value chain, final manufacturing, suppliers, R&D, technologies.”

Provost added: “I’m not here to demand whatsoever, but I think if UK is willing to join this ecosystem of IAA, there is some open question about the level of imports.”

London has so far rejected pressure to impose its own tariffs on Chinese imports, but the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, this month said that decision was under review .

Cappellano also said the UK should consider imposing tariffs on Chinese imports. “It’s very important that the UK defines what is the priority,” he said. “It’s very difficult to defend industrial footprint and at the same time let the market completely open to import. Either one or the other.”

He expressed scepticism over whether other countries beyond the EU such as Japan, Turkey and Morocco should be included in the rules.

“We don’t necessarily need to have a larger definition of European scope,” he said, pointing to proposals that carmakers be allowed to source 30% of their materials from outside the EU.

He also argued for more time until 2030 for manufacturers to source batteries from within Europe. China is dominant in the global supply of batteries and Cappellano said it would take longer to build up the European industry.

stories.title: Welsh government and Labour strike budget deal with £60m for additional learning needs
stories.summary: The Plaid Cymru-led administration had failed to pass its spending plans during the summer.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Plaid Cymru-led administration has agreed to fund an extra £60m for children with additional learning needs

Published 13 October 2026, 10:00 BST

The Welsh government has reached a deal with Labour on its mini-budget, which had failed to pass in the summer.

Ministers said the Plaid Cymru-led administration had now agreed an extra £60m for the education of children with additional learning needs (ALN).

Labour, which sits in opposition after losing May's Senedd election, had rejected a £40m a year deal across three years, in angry scenes at the Welsh Parliament in the last week of term in July.

Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates had demanded £100m this year when the supplementary budget was last discussed.

Reform said the deal was good for Plaid and Labour but not Wales.

Despite the agreement with Labour, headteachers union NAHT expressed "deep disappointment" at the level of funding.

Drakeford says Labour made mistakes in failed mini-budget talks Published 28 September

The budget will be debated in the Senedd on 3 November.

On Tuesday, First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: "This agreement reflects what can be achieved when parties across the Senedd work together."

Skates said Labour had "managed to secure a significant cash injection for schools".

"While we still believe the Welsh government should be setting aside more for ALN in schools, it is a welcome first step in dealing with the need to better fund schools," he said.

Plaid Cymru's original mini-budget included £100m for the NHS to bring down waiting times, £55m for childcare and £40m for school repairs.

If the supplementary budget is not passed then the government would have to find other ways to fund its new plans.

Helen Jenner, leader of Reform Wales, said: "While we welcome extra support for additional learning needs provision, the Welsh government is still sending millions of pounds of taxpayers' money overseas while our public services suffer here at home."

Former Welsh Labour leader Mark Drakeford previously said his party had made mistakes in how it handled negotiations with Plaid over the summer, and suggested there was a case to be made to take the money that had been previously offered by Plaid.

Following Tuesday's announcement, Llŷr Powell, Reform's chief whip, said: "When Mark Drakeford speaks, Ken Skates starts dancing."

Darren Millar, leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd, said the deal was "merely a continuation of the same failed budget approach by the Labour-Plaid duopoly that has been letting down the people of Wales for decades".

It is not known yet if Labour will vote for or abstain on the budget as part of the deal.

If Labour abstain Plaid would need the support of the Greens and Lib Dem MS Jane Dodds

Skates did not say which way his party would go, telling BBC Wales on Tuesday: "We're going to make a final decision on that but certainly we will not stop the budget from passing."

Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates had demanded £100m a year for ALN before accepting the government's £60m offer

ALN is the equivalent education system in Wales to special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) in England.

The Welsh government received extra cash as a result of more SEND spending in England to help schools struggling with debt, and Labour had argued for some of that to be given to schools in Wales.

Rob Kelsall, assistant general secretary of NAHT, said school leaders across Wales would be asking "what happened to the £322m that became available to Wales as a result of additional SEND funding in England?"

He said: "What has emerged is a package that falls substantially short of that figure and asks schools to be grateful for receiving only a fraction of what should have been available to learners with additional needs."

Welsh Education Minister, Anna Brychan, said ministers remained in "active discussions" with NAHT Cymru.

She said ALN was a "key priority" for her, and she recognised the "significant financial and operational pressures" facing schools and colleges.

"It is my hope that this additional funding, to be used in-year, will alleviate some of the more immediate financial and operational pressures facing schools, colleges, local authorities and support services," she added.

There were angry scenes in the Senedd in July when the Plaid Cymru government brought its supplementary budget to a vote without a deal in place.

Plaid failed to get any opposition support for the package.

Finance Minister Elin Jones accused Labour of behaving as a "destructive opposition" at the time.

Tory Senedd leader Millar said the decision to vote on the budget anyway was "bonkers".

The first minister later said his government had learned "lessons" from the episode, and promised to improve the way his government engaged with others.

It was not clear if the £60m offered in the deal is annual, and Brychan said allocation for future years would be part of the preparations for the draft budget for 2027-28.

Talks are ongoing with other parties for the Welsh government's full annual spending plans, which will be voted on by the Senedd early next year.

Of the £60m, £56m will be split between schools and councils - 80% to schools and 20% to councils.

Another £1.5m will be spent on a long-term sustainability plan, and £2.5m for the further education sector.

stories.title: UK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next year
stories.summary: The prediction from the IMF comes as final preparations are being made for the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 13 October 2026, 03:00 BST

The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit the economy in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said.

The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.

Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain".

Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget.

Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October.

Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money.

But IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told BBC News on Tuesday that the UK's process of managing its debts is now leading the major G7 economies.

"As you know, the UK has already started the consolidation process and it is the country that basically stands out, along with India", she said.

The organisation said the UK is one of the only major economies on course to stabilise levels of national debt. The UK is also projected to have the lowest annual borrowing in the G7 in 2031.

Asked if the UK was one of the countries the IMF was telling to reduce borrowing, Tenreyro said that the country had begun the process already and should "stay the course".

The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economies to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels.

While the IMF's forecasts are closely watched, the figures are only a prediction, a best estimate, of what will happen in the future. Forecasts often turn out to be incorrect due to world events.

Also, the chancellor's spending decisions at the Budget will be based on predictions from the UK's official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, not the IMF.

The predictions in the IMF's latest World Economic Outlook suggest:

the UK is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany

UK growth is set to slow next year to 1.2% as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates hit household spending and business investment

UK inflation is expected to average 3.3% this year, and the IMF has increased its forecast for inflation next year to 2.8%.

the IMF said the global economy was "proving resilient" despite the ongoing war in the Middle East, helped by the investment surge in AI.

Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF Published 11 hours ago

What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 9 hours ago

'Slow bicycle race'

Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience".

When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks.

Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, told the BBC the IMF's growth forecast was "better than it might have been", but noted that for 2027 it remained "more pessimistic".

"We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are," he added.

Sir Howard said the UK was "a bit of a sideshow" when it comes to the global economy and the IMF was more focused on how much the US is adding to its debt pile.

"That is what is putting pressure on interest rates all over the world and that is what is affecting us as well. Unless the US does something about its deficit, we can expect interest rates to be higher, which of course increases our debt interest costs," he said.

He added that the IMF was giving the UK credit in its forecast for tax rises which it might not end up actually putting through.

Economists have suggested Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget.

On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes".

Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it".
