stories.title: Chronic UTIs made MP 'feel like a drug user'
stories.summary: Dr Allison Gardner MP has been living with the "searing pain" of recurring infections for a decade.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Dr Allison Gardner, the Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent South, is leading a group of MPs to improve recognition of chronic UTIs

Published 13 October 2026, 06:38 BST

Warning: This story contains reference to suicide

An MP says she was left "feeling like a drug user" while trying desperately to find pain relief for chronic urinary tract infections (UTIs).

Labour MP Dr Allison Gardner has been living with the "searing pain" of recurrent infections for about 10 years, after first experiencing symptoms with perimenopause.

According to the Chronic Urinary Tract Infection Campaign (CUTIC), more than 1.6 million women in the UK suffer from chronic lower urinary tract symptoms, but there is no official medical definition of the condition.

That is something Gardner is trying to change, with the support of a cross party group of MPs in Parliament.

Gardner told the BBC how a lack of consensus on what constituted a chronic UTI left her feeling sidelined by doctors, who did not always understand the condition and were limited in the length of antibiotic courses they could prescribe.

"You end up hunting for a decent length of antibiotic courses that will give you some relief," she said.

UTIs are caused by bacteria entering the urethra , external . As women have a shorter urethra than men, bacteria are more likely to reach the bladder or kidneys and cause an infection.

Chronic UTIs are infections where symptoms do not go away, and do not clear with a short course of antibiotics. They can also be difficult to diagnose, due to a lower level of bacteria shown in urine samples.

Gardner told the BBC she had considered selling her home to pay for bladder removal surgery after years of pain

"It's a searing pain every time you go to the loo" said Gardner, 60. "It's just like hot needles being inserted inside you and just burning, burning, burning."

She told the BBC she had felt "gaslighted" by medics and had been told to "wipe yourself better" after describing intense pain.

She was even told by one consultant to give up sex because it can cause a flare up.

"You've got to fight all the time just to get treated sensibly and [not told] you've got anxiety, depression or are attention seeking," Gardner said.

The pain and lack of answers about her condition eventually led her to a very dark place.

"It got to the point where [I thought] 'if this is how my life is going to be, I can't carry on'," she said.

She was so desperate she even considered selling her house to pay for private surgery to have her bladder removed.

It was around that time three years ago that she discovered Dr Cat Anderson, a Staffordshire-based GP who works in private practice and for the NHS.

She was the first to identify that Gardner's symptoms were related to the menopause and prescribed her Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT).

"I had two years free of UTI - I just had my life back," said Gardner.

Asked whether going private went against her Labour principles that healthcare should be free, Gardner said: "You're stuck with a choice aren't you?

"You either suffer or you go private... so I don't judge."

She added that she believed everyone should have access to the healthcare they needed.

Anderson specialises in challenging UTI cases, and is leading a group of medical experts to develop a medical definition of chronic UTIs to differentiate it from other conditions.

The panel hope that an official definition will pave the way for better diagnosis and treatment.

Persistent infections, Anderson said, could "ruin a patient's quality of life" - limiting their ability to work or do something as simple as pick their children up from school.

She has also seen people "who are quite literally driven to suicide" due to "awful" symptoms.

Anderson specialises in recurrent UTIs and is working with other doctors to develop a medical definition for the condition

The expert medical panel that Anderson heads up with Sachin Malde, a London-based consultant urological surgeon, is planning to deliver its official definition of chronic UTI in 2027. This will then be presented to the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE).

As to why there is no current definition of chronic UTI, NICE said it had recommended further research into chronic UTIs to develop a "clear evidence base" for any recommendations.

A spokesperson for NHS England also confirmed that currently there was no single national dataset that specifically captured all cases of chronic UTI as a distinct clinical diagnosis.

"This is not just a 'nice to do', this would be transformational - not just within the UK, but globally," said Gardner, of the work she is doing with other MPs in the All Party Parliamentary Group (APPG).

In 2023-24, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) found that UTIs accounted for 1.2 million hospital bed days, costing hospitals and the NHS more than £604m.

Dr Ron Daniels, founder and chief medical officer of the UK Sepsis Trust, said as many as 20% of all sepsis cases - which can prove fatal - are thought to originate from the urinary tract.

Gardner and Anderson hope a formal definition of chronic UTIs will pave the way for better treatment

Beyond the definition and improving diagnosis and treatment, the APPG wants to see all GPs trained on chronic UTIs and introduce a "passport" for patients so they do not have to repeatedly explain their medical history.

In April, then-health secretary Wes Streeting said the NHS had an "appalling culture of medical misogyny" , external where being "ignored, gaslit, humiliated and disrespected, were common experiences for far too many women".

Liberal Democrat MP Luke Taylor, who co-chairs the APPG with Gardner, said the group was "disappointed" that Streeting's announcement of the women's health strategy "didn't even mention UTIs, let alone chronic UTIs".

The group, he said, has now set its sights on lobbying the government to invest in research and improve care.

When we asked the Department of Health and Social Care what specific improvements patients with chronic UTIs might see, a spokesperson said they were committed to "reducing the impact" chronic UTIs have on people's lives and had invested in research "to ensure that women are listened to at every stage, and given access to the high-quality care they need".

stories.title: Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again
stories.summary: For the first time since the UK left the EU, we have a prime minister who will "unflinchingly" debate Brexit, says the BBC's political editor Chris Mason.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 13 October 2026, 02:27 BST

The Brexit debate is back.

For years, it felt like the only thing Westminster talked about.

I have had a ringside seat at it all, from the Conservative election victory in 2015, with the party's promise in its manifesto that year to offer "a straight in-out referendum on our membership of the European Union by the end of 2017."

Then there was the then Prime Minister David Cameron's negotiation with the European Union to try to secure what he saw as a better deal and then the referendum itself on Thursday, 23 June 2016.

And that, you will remember, was merely the start, as years of wrangling began. Two general elections came and went in 2017 and 2019 and it took the two prime ministers after David Cameron, first Theresa May and then Boris Johnson, before the UK left the European Union at 23:00 on Friday, 31 January 2020.

Little wonder perhaps that by that point, almost irrespective of someone's views on the topic, there was an appetite to talk about something else. Anything else. Political parties picked up that vibe and while their long standing instincts on the EU were there to see if you scratched the surface, there was minimal desire to extemporise about them any time soon.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Burnham: Post-Brexit status quo with Europe 'not good enough for Britain'

With the arrival of Andy Burnham as prime minister, that has changed, despite what he said just a few months before he arrived in Downing Street.

He has been happy to repeatedly lean into an argument claiming that it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain." First he made this case at the Labour Party Conference last month and now he has made it again in the House of Commons.

Burnham is attempting to make a two-pronged case.

First, in the short term, he wants to "deepen" the UK's relationship with the EU at a summit in Brussels at the end of next month. He insists such a deepening would be within the promise made by Labour at the last general election that the UK would say no to the customs union, the single market and freedom of movement.

Which brings us onto the second element of his case, in the medium term. What might Labour promise in its next general election manifesto? The prime minister told me a fortnight ago the manifesto could promise an in-out referendum.

In the Commons, he sought to reassure you, whatever your view on Brexit.

"This country in the next decade needs to know where it's going. There are no assumptions here, and as I said, the British public will be the boss of whatever is decided," he said.

Hang on, say critics, it was decided by voters a decade ago.

"They weighed the arguments and made a decision. The least they are owed is politicians willing to defend it," argues Lord Frost , external , a former Brexit minister and chief Brexit negotiator in the Telegraph.

The focus of the next five weeks, ahead of a UK-EU Summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November, is what Downing Street sees as short term wins on youth mobility, food and drink, and energy.

Andy Burnham hopes to make an argument that what he will portray as a sensible, pragmatic deepening of the relationship with Brussels can help cut illegal immigration and boost economic growth.

He sought to goad the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch for seeking to oppose a plan he thinks can contribute to growth. She argued it risked regurgitating yesterday's arguments with little prospect of success.

And, strikingly, his attempt at goading his opponents went further still. He told The Rest Is Politics podcast that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there was Russian interference in the Brexit referendum.

"I've had a clear answer that, yes, there was," he claimed, without saying who provided that clear answer or what the evidence for that suggested clarity was.

In the Commons, his language appeared a little softer. He told MPs it was "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere. A double negative deployed this time, about alleged attempts at interference.

His political opponents were already pouncing. The Reform UK leader Nigel Farage was blunt – calling the prime minister "a liar."

The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson added that he had asked the same question as Andy Burnham did when he became Foreign Secretary , external "and they replied that there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: PM says there is 'clear' evidence of Russian interference in 2016 Brexit campaign

And so a debate resumes about the difference between attempted interference, interference and successful interference.

But the key point is this: for the first time since the UK left the European Union, we now have a prime minister who is willing to unflinchingly debate Brexit: whether it is working, how it is working, how to improve it, and if it's proved to be a failure.

In so doing he hopes he can tap into public sentiment. Opinion polls suggest a perception among a majority that leaving the European Union has not turned out how many might have hoped.

On top of this, he hopes to lure pro Europeans broadly on the Left who may recently have supported the Liberal Democrats, the Green parties of both England and Wales and Scotland, the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru towards Labour. That is the political logic from the government's point of view, for now at least.

And as for where all of this leads – well, good question. In the coming weeks, months and perhaps years, there may be a Back to the Future vibe to our political debate. A splash of familiarity, as a conversation about the relationship we have with our nearest neighbours resumes.

stories.body:
Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%

Business live – latest updates

VW boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic industry

The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.

Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year.

The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week .

The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.

Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.

Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars in China will.

China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data.

As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.

Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing.

“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said.

Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the “Made in Europe” legislation would do the same in public procurement.

On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.

after newsletter promotion

The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.

Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China.

Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.

“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official.

Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU.

“I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said.

stories.body:
Thinktank’s influential pre-budget report urges key decisions to be made now and not put off until next year

John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures.

As the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade.

Against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, the thinktank warned Healey that failure to address the issue at his 28 October budget risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans.

Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.”

Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at Jeremy Hunt , the former Conservative chancellor, who before the 2024 general election was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans.

Publishing its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances before Healey’s speech to the Commons, it called on the chancellor to avoid announcing a “steady as she goes” budget that delayed decisions until next year’s spending review.

“If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said.

Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.”

Miller said the Treasury adopting an assumption that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility.

“We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.”

Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30.

With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement.

Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash.

The IFS said that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue – meaning Healey could see headroom cut by only £4bn.

after newsletter promotion

However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services.

Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing.

The IFS said a choice to leave spending totals unchanged at the budget would implicitly mean allowing the quality or quantity of public services to fall. However, it said compensating for the inflation shock, and funding Healey’s pledge to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, would require tax rises or benefit cuts of about £35bn.

“Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said.

“It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.”

She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within.

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “The chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.

“The Office for Budget Responsibility will publish its updated forecast alongside the budget in October and we will not comment on rumour, speculation or proposals about its contents ahead of then.”

stories.title: Attorney General approval required for serious Troubles prosecutions
stories.summary: It is among a series of amendments the government has tabled for its bill, which seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the decades-long violent conflict.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The bill was first introduced to Parliament last year following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government

Published 12 October 2026

The Attorney General must provide consent for any serious prosecutions related to the Troubles in Northern Ireland, under changes to the government's planned legislation.

It is among a series of amendments the government has tabled for its bill, which seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the decades-long violent conflict.

The bill was first introduced to Parliament last year following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government.

Northern Ireland secretary Sir Chris Bryant said the amendments give "robust, permanent safeguards" to ensure former soldiers and police officers are treated with "fairness, dignity and respect".

The Labour government has faced criticism over delays in passing the bill as well as questions over some of its contents.

It seeks to replace the previous Conservative government's contentious 2023 Legacy Act, which introduced a ban on inquests and civil actions related to Troubles-era incidents.

The act's most controversial element - offering immunity from prosecution to suspects who cooperated with an information recovery body - was disapplied after being found by the courts to be unlawful.

Labour's bill involves a Legacy Commission to investigate Troubles-related killings, a separate information recovery body, and a dedicated legacy unit within An Garda Síochána (Irish police).

The government said its amendments "significantly reduce" the prospect of military veterans facing "rinse and repeat" investigations.

While some MPs have previously argued that planned protections for veterans do not go far enough, Stormont's First Minister Michelle O'Neill has accused the government of giving former soldiers "preferential treatment".

The government said the amendments include:

The legislation will make clear the Commission and coroners "must not regard the lawful conduct of members of the Armed Forces as equivalent to the actions of paramilitaries responsible for acts of terrorism"

The Attorney General will be required to consent to all "serious" Troubles-related prosecutions

Measures to prevent "cold-calling" of veterans and extending provisions for remote attendance as part of the Commission's work

Before any witness can be approached, the Commission should consider if "compelling new evidence exists, or the likelihood of a witness being able to provide new information"

The Commission must consider the "context and command orders" in which military veterans were operating

Former paramilitaries barred from being appointed to the Victims and Survivors Advisory Group, and a requirement for at least one veteran or veterans' representative to be on the panel

A statutory review of the measures for veterans to ensure they "deliver as intended"

Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said he is "confident that this legislation will be a significant step towards a more reconciled society"

Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said the bill was about completing the "unfinished business" of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement peace deal.

"I am confident that this legislation will be a significant step towards a more reconciled society," he said in a statement.

Bryant said the "significant package of amendments" would provide "robust, permanent safeguards that ensure former Armed Forces personnel and police officers are treated with the fairness, dignity, and respect they deserve".

He added: "These amendments have been developed through extensive engagement with veterans' groups, whilst ensuring that this bill will also enable victims and bereaved families, including the families of soldiers, who have waited long years for answers, to seek information and, potentially, closure, on what happened to their loved ones."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said "the amendments will help ensure that decisions on historic cases properly take account of the operational realities faced by our Armed Forces"

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that "for too long, veterans have faced uncertainty over historic investigations, despite serving honourably during the Troubles".

"The amendments will help ensure that decisions on historic cases properly take account of the operational realities faced by our Armed Forces, who often make split-second decisions in exceptionally difficult circumstances," he added.

'Preferential treatment'

The Sinn Féin MP John Finucane denounced the amendments as a "veterans' charter".

He said they "risk preferential treatment, providing additional protections for former members of the British military while placing further obstacles in the path of effective investigations".

"The requirement for the British Attorney General, who is a political appointee, to approve prosecutions raises serious questions about whether families will be able to get truth or justice," he added in a statement.

The bill is expected to be discussed in the House of Commons on Tuesday and voted on by MPs next week.

If passed it will move to the House of Lords for further consideration by peers.

stories.title: Votes of no confidence in Sinn Féin ministers fail
stories.summary: The attempt to oust them failed as it required cross-community support from a majority of both unionists and nationalists in the assembly.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The motions against Michelle O'Neill (centre), Liz Kimmins (left), John O'Dowd and Caoimhe Archibald (right) were debated after receiving the backing of unionist parties last week

Published 12 October 2026

Votes of no confidence in First Minister Michelle O'Neill and three other Sinn Féin ministers have fallen after failing to secure enough support in Stormont.

The Northern Ireland Assembly debated the no-confidence motions over the ministers' handling of the Drumcree dispute, after they received the backing of unionist parties last week .

However, the attempt to oust them failed as it required cross-community support from a majority of both unionists and nationalists in the assembly.

O'Neill described the move as "pointless" but Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said her power-sharing partner had "shattered" public confidence and needed to be held accountable.

It comes amid a major political row over a planned Orange Order march in Portadown, County Armagh.

O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin politicians have been heavily criticised by unionists for joining protests which have blocked the parade from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.

What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? Published 29 September

Four key takeaways from the Drumcree dispute so far Published 3 days ago

First minister rejects call to resign over Drumcree row Published 5 October

Police are investigating the demonstrations in a "large-scale" criminal inquiry .

The first minister again defended her involvement in blocking the Garvaghy Road during the debate, describing the planned Orange Order march as "triumphalist and sectarian".

Motions of no-confidence in the assembly are not binding without cross-community support from both unionist and nationalist MLAs, and cannot automatically force a minister from office.

TUV member Timothy Gaston tabled the no-confidence motions

Speaking during the assembly debate, Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) member Timothy Gaston, who tabled the no-confidence motions, described O'Neill as the "first minister of lawlessness" who "doesn't want an Orangeman about the place".

He asked: "If a determination can be set aside simply because republican protesters object to it, what confidence can any loyalist, any Orangeman, any unionist, have in the impartial administration of justice here in Northern Ireland?"

He said there needed to be "political consequences" for Sinn Féin and reiterated TUV's call for the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) to withdraw their deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill from the first minister post.

'Shattered'

Little-Pengelly said that people across Northern Ireland have been "appalled" by the conduct of Sinn Féin ministers.

"I would appeal to those sitting opposite to get a grip and realise that you have done damage," the DUP minister told the assembly.

"Damage to these institutions, damage to the ministerial roles that they should feel privileged to hold.

"That confidence from the people of Northern Ireland has been shattered."

Michelle O'Neill has defended her actions, saying she was "proud" to stand with the residents

O'Neill said it was "no surprise" unionist parties had supported the no-confidence motions because "they have never accepted equality".

"They have never accepted rights and respect, and again they still haven't respected the fact that it is now 2026."

The exclusion motions have also been submitted against John O'Dowd, Caoimhe Archibald and Liz Kimmins.

O'Dowd, who is also the finance minister, told the assembly he was "proud" to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents.

He accused the TUV of wanting to bring Stormont down.

Earlier, he told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme that he would continue to work with other parties.

"I am seeking engagements around the budget, I want to work with parties to make a better society for everyone."

Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said the parading dispute had been used to create "instability" and said "the days of Orange domination are done".

Kimmins, who is the infrastructure minister, added that she had seen both "some of the most regressive elements of loyalism and unionism" over recent weeks and "the very best of our communities" in support of Garvaghy Road residents.

TUV assembly member Timothy Gaston (right) alongside party leader Jim Allister

The motions gained the required 30 signatures with the backing of assembly members from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) and the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP).

Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme , the TUV leader, Jim Allister, admitted the debate was "not going to succeed succeed because of the absurd system whereby it needs cross-community support".

"But that accentuates the pressure on the DUP to be seen to do something because as things stand lawbreakers are sitting in our executive."

'Abject failure'

DUP assembly member Jonathan Buckley, who signed the no-confidence motions, accused Sinn Féin of "abject failure of political leadership".

"The genesis of today's debate may be about a parade, but it is about much more," he told the assembly.

"It is about the rule of law. It is about those who feel they are above it and not accountable to it".

Earlier, DUP leader Gavin Robinson called for sanctions to be introduced against anyone who broke the law.

Robinson said he plans to speak to the secretary of state on Monday evening to ensure that there is "accountability".

He said the legislation should be "brought forward that will bring sanctions so that anyone who has broken the law is subject to it and punished".

Regarding what actions the DUP could take, Robinson said "nothing is of the table".

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that removing Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister would "punish everybody else"

The DUP and Ulster Unionists share power with Sinn Féin in a four-party devolved government alongside the Alliance Party.

Jim Allister has been urging the DUP to withdraw Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill as first minister.

Earlier on Good Morning Ulster , Robinson had said that he is "not in the territory" to "destabilise".

However his party colleague, Carla Lockhart, who represents the Upper Bann constituency in Westminster, said it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont and the DUP has it "within its gift to remove" O'Neill from her position.

Robinson said that when the party comes to a "consensus, that is our position".

He added that Lockhart has "the right to stand up for her constituents".

DUP MP Carla Lockhart said it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont

UUP leader Jon Burrows called Sinn Féin "morally bankrupt" and said the party had "a recurring problem with accountability".

"We have a party that simply will not sign up to the normal rules of democracy," he told the assembly.

Addressing those on the Sinn Féin benches, Burrows said they should be "ashamed of their conduct".

Earlier, he told BBC Radio Ulster's Nolan Show he would not withdraw Health Minister Robbie Butler from the executive, "because to do so would affect the people of Northern Ireland in all the work he is doing".

Burrows said he was instead calling for changes to Stormont's rules, and said there should be "proper accountability mechanisms" to hold ministers who breach the pledge of office to account.

'Depressing, dispiriting'

Alliance Party deputy leader Eóin Tennyson branded the no-confidence motions a "political stunt" designed to collapse Stormont.

Tennyson described the debate as "depressing, dispiriting and almost unbelievable", warning that power-sharing institutions were "once again being placed in jeopardy".

However, he also said any elected representatives found to have acted unlawfully in recent weeks "should face the consequences of that conduct".

Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) assembly member Matthew O'Toole, leader of Stormont's official opposition, welcomed the NI Secretary's decision to ban the Drumcree parade, a dispute which he said had "opened up deep wounds that didn't need to be reopened".

O'Toole said he was not "diminishing or trivialising the rule of law" and his party would "cooperate" with investigations.

"Because we do accept the rule of law and the need for the PSNI and the courts to do their job," he added.

"But we were also founded, the SDLP, in the tradition of peaceful protest.

"That's in our DNA and that right is sacrosanct, and sometimes such action is unavoidable."

stories.body:
With the cash rate at a 15-year high, consumer confidence has tanked – while household spending is still growing

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Interest rates have risen to 15-year highs and are pushing up mortgage default risks – but household spending is still growing.

Economists say the surprising result shows this year’s four rate hikes have not yet fully hit the economy and may be less effective at fighting inflation than they used to be. If true, that could mean more interest rate rises are on the way.

So are interest rate hikes working?

What is the RBA trying to achieve by increasing interest rates?

The Reserve Bank has increased its key cash rate to cut household spending and discourage businesses and workers from seeking higher prices and wages. It aims to bring inflation back under 3%.

Financial institutions now face higher funding costs and have responded by lifting the rates they charge for home loans, business loans or bonds for big companies.

But eight months on from the year’s first rate rise in February, spending is not going backwards.

Economic activity has slowed, businesses are less efficient and real wages are going backwards compared with a year ago as inflation rises. But Australian household spending has accelerated, up nearly 7% compared with a year ago, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics estimates.

Part of the increase in spending is from higher prices for essentials such as fuel and food. But it also reflects strong demand for electric cars and non-essentials – particularly overseas travel .

Inflation has risen to 4% as of August, both because of oil disruption and mass construction of big projects like datacentres and because local businesses are lifting their prices. When customers are willing to spend big, businesses find it easier to raise prices.

Do higher mortgage rates cut household budgets?

The cash rate’s most immediate effect is on household cashflow, taking money away from borrowers while giving more to debt-free savers.

RBA data shows higher rates and prices have left 2% of borrowers unable to afford essential expenses but most people are meeting repayments.

Warren Hogan, the managing director of EQ Economics, says the emergence of mortgage offset accounts in the last decade has reduced rates’ effect on cashflow. Borrowers who have spare cash in offset accounts, often because they can afford to pay more than their minimum, now have “massive buffers”. Australians now hold nearly $350bn in total in offset balances .

“You just didn’t have the same amount of capacity to pay off earlier and have offsets accounts and all that sort of thing,” Hogan says.

Home ownership is in decline, meaning more Australians are renters whose spending is not directly hit by higher mortgage rates.

One in three households own their home debt-free and benefit from higher interest on their savings. Commonwealth Bank data indicates older Australians and debt-free homeowners have steadily increased their spending this year.

Will falling house prices discourage spending?

The slide in house prices is a sign that interest rates and higher borrowing costs are directly restricting economic activity, according to David Bassanese, the chief economist at BetaShares.

House price slides are also an indirect channel for hikes to slow spending as homeowners tend to cut back when falls in home values make them less wealthy than they had been. RBA research suggests a 10% fall in housing prices – which is expected by mid-2027 – will cut consumption by 1.5%.

Bassanese says consumer spending does not appear to have slowed yet by as much as past RBA models would imply. “We’re probably not seeing a major effect yet, but in theory, it should be starting to happen,” he said.

The “wealth effect” of interest rates is typically slower-moving than the cashflow effect.

But most homeowners are also wealthier than they were two years ago, with the median national price back to where it was in September.

What about exchange rates?

The Reserve Bank says the most important effect of interest rate rises is through the exchange rate. Higher interest rates tend to push up demand to invest in Australia, lifting the Australian dollar, making imports cheaper.

But the dollar has been fairly stable against other currencies because foreign central banks like the US Federal Reserve are also lifting their own interest rates.

The Australian dollar rose from 65 US cents in November 2025 to 72 in May 2026, after the first three RBA rate rises but has fallen to 69 US cents. It has followed a similar path compared to an index of Australia’s trade partners, including China, Japan, Europe and South Korea.

“We’re raising rates, but so is everybody else,” Bassanese says. “Our currency is not especially strong, although it has lifted somewhat over the past year.”

How does higher unemployment stop inflation?

Interest rate rises aim to push up unemployment but the hikes have had little effect this year.

More jobseekers make it easier for businesses to find workers without lifting wages. Higher wages would be passed on as higher prices for customers, so more unemployment tends to mean less inflation.

But the jobs market has been surprisingly strong. Health and care sectors have rapidly hired thanks to bigger demand and government subsidies while productivity is going backwards, forcing businesses to hire more workers to keep up production.

The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, has said she wants to see a small increase in jobless rates so there is less pressure from wages on prices, drawing criticism from unions.

Unemployment increasing from 4.6% to 5% would represent an extra 60,000 people out of work if the workforce stayed the same size.

But Bullock said after September’s rate hike that she does not expect job losses, instead hoping job creation will slow and more people will look to join the workforce, leaving jobseekers searching for longer periods.

Markets expect only one more rate rise and not until May 2027. But the Deutsche Bank strategist Lachlan Dynan warns rate rises’ weaker effects add to the risk of another hike.

“The Australian household sector has been more resilient to hikes than many expected,” Dynan says. “Risks to RBA [rates] are back to being skewed to the upside in our view.”

stories.title: Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, Miliband says as he summons Iran ambassador
stories.summary: The prime minister says Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard "almost certainly" directed the RAF Fairford incident.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A large cordon was put in place around the base and dozens of homes were evacuated

Published 12 October 2026

The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's incident at RAF Fairford.

Ed Miliband said attempts by Iran to undermine the UK's security "through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs the incident in Gloucestershire was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard", while the home secretary said the likely coordinator was a "known individual based in Iran".

Iran's ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Tehran was not involved and was willing to cooperate with British authorities.

The Foreign Office has also sanctioned two Iranians, including the head of the regime's counterespionage operations - with both men subjected to travel bans and asset freezes.

Burnham also indicated Iran could be hit with further sanctions over its suspected role.

It comes as the UK and 28 other countries - including the US, Canada, Australia, France and Germany - issued a joint statement condemning "in the strongest terms" violent attacks by Iran.

The statement accuses Tehran of carrying out "lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities" and also recognises the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

A huge police operation began after officers were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base in the early hours of 27 September.

Dozens of homes were evacuated in the nearby village of Whelford and a large cordon was put in place around the site.

So far, a total of seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged.

Last week, Downing Street insisted the airbase was safe after the US withdrew all of its bombers – about a dozen B-1s from the base – back to their home stations on American soil.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

RAF Fairford, in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved an American request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

A US state department spokesman confirmed that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had a call with Miliband on Monday where they discussed "holding Iran to account for its actions and of continued collaboration to secure US assets in the United Kingdom".

stories.title: Government expands police support to political figures who are not MPs
stories.summary: Shabana Mahmood says there is "insufficient protection" for those who play a role in public life.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 12 October 2026

Political figures who are not currently MPs will be given police support, the home secretary has announced.

Shabana Mahmood told MPs there was "insufficient protection" for those serving in public life and that the new announcement will cover peers, former MPs and party spokespeople.

She also announced an urgent, independent review of security arrangements for high-profile figures including politicians and royals.

It comes three months after Reform UK spokeswoman and former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home in Devon, having been hit on the head with a hammer 21 times as she ate lunch.

Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with her murder, and he was also charged with preparing acts of terror against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Kerry is alleged to have carried out research on prominent targets over a period of two years, including trying to gain entry into Farage's London home.

Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Mahmood said that "robust debate and criticism are part of this job - threats, abuse and violence are not."

She did not elaborate on what the support would involve, but told MPs it would include access to a named police officer and help with wider security measures.

The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years, following the murders of Conservative MP Sir David Amess in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox in 2016.

"We owe it to them and to everyone who believes in a fair and open country to ensure that those who serve at all levels receive the protection they deserve," Mahmood added.

The "root and branch" independent review into security arrangements will be led by former national security advisor Stephen Lovegrove, and will look into "physical threats, online risks and the dangers posed within our more polarised society".

Mahmood confirmed that the review will report within six months, and build on the existing work of Sir Robert Buckland, who is leading a separate review into the murder of Sir David.

In response, shadow home secretary Chris Philp welcomed the extension of protective measures, saying threats to elected representatives are threats to democracy.

Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf welcomed the review, but added: "It is disappointing that it took the murder of one of our colleagues, countless threats towards our party spokespeople and months of campaigning from Reform UK to make this government take action."

Reform has in recent months accused the government of a "dereliction of duty" over Farage's taxpayer-funded security, claiming it had previously been "downgraded" - a charge that the Home Office has said is "categorically untrue".

Decisions over the security of current MPs and members of the House of Lords are made by the House of Parliament's security team.

There is a separate, independent committee, the Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec), to deal with high-profile political candidates, which is staffed by officials from the Home Office, the Cabinet Office, and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.

The Jo Cox Foundation welcomed the home secretary's announcement but said "strengthening physical security" alone was not enough.

"We must also tackle the root causes - including online harms and education - to prevent future attacks," its chief executive Olivia Field said in a statement on X.

According to data released to the BBC in April , the number of alleged offences against MPs have increased year-on-year, with 976 recorded in 2025, compared to 364 in 2019.

MPs reported 4,064 crimes to the Met's Parliamentary Liaison Team between 2019 and 2025. Most offences were related to malicious communications followed by harassment, and criminal damage to a building.

In 2025, there were 50 death threats reported - up from 31 the previous year.

Li Cunxin has now written two. The renowned ballet dancer and former artistic director of Queensland Ballet had hoped he was finished writing his story after the phenomenal international success of his 2003 memoir, Mao’s Last Dancer. But life had other plans. “Actually, I had signed a contract with Penguin Random House for a follow-up,” Cunxin says, from his home in Brisbane. “It was going to be about the lives of my brothers and friends in China, and the ways the country has changed over time. stories.title: Send us your questions for economist Isabella Weber on inflation and affordability
stories.summary: First Edition newsletter will be hosting a reader Q&A with economist Isabella Weber, a leading voice on inflation, affordability and cost of living and now’s your chance to put your questions to her Isabella Weber is one of the most sought-after and influential economists of her generation, and has advised policymakers and governments in the US, Germany, Europe and Latin America. She has become a leading voice on inflation , affordability and the cost of living. Her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics, looks at the relationship between economic insecurity and the rise of the far right, arguing progressive politics must respond to the rise of authoritarianism by urgently addressing the economic pressures people experience in their daily lives. For years Weber was treated as an outlier. Weber is an associate professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and an associate in research at Harvard’s Fairbank Center, and is the author of the prize-winning How China Escaped Shock Therapy. We’d love to hear your questions. Perhaps you would like to find out how the cost of living affects the current political landscape? What’s happening in the bond markets? Or the advice she’d give to progressive politicians, from incumbents like Burnham and Mamdani to the German parties taking on the AFD.
